title: Chapter 38: The Stalk of Grass 6
content:
Chapter 38

Lan Wangji materialized like a localized blizzard, stepping squarely between Wei Wuxian and the threat. Xue Yang hurled Shuanghua forward to parry the strike, the two legendary blades colliding in a brilliant, ringing clash before rebounding back into their wielders' grips.

Wei Wuxian couldn't help but chime in, "Talk about immaculate timing!"

"Mm," Lan Wangji replied simply.

Without another word, he pressed the offensive. Seconds earlier, Xue Yang had been hounding Wei Wuxian across every corner of the room; now, under Lan Wangji’s suffocating pressure, he was the one driven steadily onto his back foot. Sensing the tide turning against him, Xue Yang’s eyes flicked sideways with a devious smirk. Tossing Shuanghua from his right hand to catch it cleanly in his left, he shook his right sleeve, letting a second longsword slide effortlessly into his grip to pivot into a fluid, ambidextrous assault.

Though his sleeves appeared slim and tailored for combat, they were clearly modified spatial cuffs. The blade he’d drawn radiated a grim, sinister chill that stood in stark, jarring contrast to Shuanghua’s pure, celestial silver. Dual-wielding with effortless, deadly coordination, Xue Yang surged back onto the offensive.

Lan Wangji’s eyes narrowed slightly. "Jiangzai?"

"Oh?" Xue Yang grinned. "Hanguang-jun recognizes my blade? What an honor."

Jiangzai—literally "to bring down calamity"—was Xue Yang’s personal spiritual sword. A weapon that lived up to its name: just like its master, it was an omen of slaughter and soaked in blood.

Wei Wuxian tossed in his two cents from the sidelines. "A match made in heaven, really."

Lan Wangji didn't break focus. "Fall back. You are not needed here."

Happy to take solid advice, Wei Wuxian retreated without a fuss. Drifting toward the threshold, he glanced outside. Wen Ning was deadpan as ever, hoisting Song Lan by the throat and slamming him into a brick wall with enough concussive force to crater the masonry into a human silhouette. Song Lan, equally expressionless, twisted his wrist in a lightning counter-grip and flipped Wen Ning clean into the pavement. The two fierce corpses traded earth-shattering blows with zero vocal commentary, completely numb to pain and indifferent to damage. Short of being hacked into confetti, missing limbs would hardly slow them down.

Wei Wuxian muttered under his breath, "Guess they don't need me out here either."

Right then, across the dark street in a shuttered storefront, he caught sight of Lan Jingyi waving at him like a drowning man.Ah, now that's where I'm needed.

The second Wei Wuxian cleared the threshold, Bichen flared with blinding radiance. Caught off guard, Xue Yang's grip slipped, and Shuanghua spun out of his hand, slicing through the air. Lan Wangji snatched it cleanly out of midair.

Seeing Shuanghua fall into enemy hands, Xue Yang slashed Jiangzai straight toward Lan Wangji’s left arm to sever it. When the strike missed, a flash of venomous, icy rage tore across Xue Yang’s eyes. He growled through his teeth, "Give me that sword."

Lan Wangji leveled a cold stare at him. "You are unworthy of it."

Xue Yang let out a vicious scoff.

Over in the opposite storefront, the young disciples swarmed Wei Wuxian the second he stepped inside. "Everyone still in one piece?" he asked.

"We're fine!"

"Did just what you said—held our breath the whole time."

"Good," Wei Wuxian said. "Step out of line, and I'm forcing another bowl of that spicy congee down your throat."

The boys who’d tasted his culinary disaster gagged in collective horror.

Right then, a dull rumble of approaching footsteps echoed from every direction. Down at the far end of the avenue, dark figures were already swarming through the gloom.

Catching the sound, Lan Wangji snapped his sleeve, summoning the Wangji guqin across a wooden table with a hollow thud. Flipping Bichen into his left hand to keep Xue Yang’s dual-swords at bay, he swept his right hand out blindly, raking his fingers across the zither strings.

The chords rang out sharp and crystalline, rolling down the avenue like rolling thunder, met instantly by the familiar, wet bursts of exploding corpse heads in the distance. He traded blistering swordplay with his left hand while his right plucked effortlessly across the strings, casually reading the room and tossing off lethal musical strikes with unshakeable poise.

Jin Ling couldn't stop himself from blurting out, "Incredible!"

Growing up watching Jiang Cheng and Jin Guangyao lead night-hunts and dispatch monstrous beasts, he had always viewed his two uncles as the absolute pinnacle of the cultivation world. For Lan Wangji, he had only ever felt dread—terrified of the man's icy glare and zero-tolerance Silence Spells. But watching him effortlessly command the field now, Jin Ling was thoroughly captivated.

Lan Jingyi puffed out his chest, gloating, "Of course he is! Hanguang-jun is peerless—he just doesn't go around bragging about it like some people. Super humble, right?"

The "right?" was aimed dead at Wei Wuxian.

Wei Wuxian blinked. "Are you asking me? Why ask me?"

Jingyi bristled. "What, you don't think Hanguang-jun is incredible?!"

Wei Wuxian rubbed his chin, a fond grin creeping up his face. "Sure, sure. Amazing. Brilliant. He's the greatest."

The night of near-misses was winding down, and dawn was peeking over the horizon. But sunrise was hardly good news. Daylight meant the supernatural smog would only thicken, blinding them completely!

If it were just him and Lan Wangji, slipping away would be trivial. But with a flock of living disciples in tow, getting encircled by a massive horde of corpses would leave them dead in the water.

While Wei Wuxian scrambled for a way out, that rhythmic, hollow tapping of bamboo against flagstones echoed down the lane once more.

The blind, mute spirit was back!

Wei Wuxian made the call on the spot. "Move!"

"Move where?" Jingyi asked.

"Follow that tapping."

Jin Ling stared at him in disbelief. "You want us to tail a ghost? Who knows where she's leading us!"

"We follow her," Wei Wuxian insisted. "She's been shadowing you since you entered the city, right? You were trying to head deeper into town, but she kept steering you back toward the gates until you ran into us. She wasn't stalking you—she was trying to chase you out to save your lives!"

That creepy, elusive tapping had just been her crude way of spooking mortals away from danger. Even that severed paper head Wei Wuxian had tripped over earlier had likely been tossed in their path as a warning scare.

Wei Wuxian pressed on, "Plus, she was desperately trying to warn us about something earlier, but couldn't get it across. And the second Xue Yang showed his face, she vanished. Ten to one, she’s hiding from him. She is definitely not on his side."

"Wait, Xue Yang?! Where did Xue Yang come from?! Weren't we dealing with Xiao Xingchen and Song Lan?"

"I'll explain later! Bottom line: the guy trading blows with Hanguang-jun isn't Xiao Xingchen—it's Xue Yang wearing his face."

The bamboo stick tapped persistently against the stone, somewhere between waiting and urging them to hurry. Following her carried risks, but staying put meant getting suffocated in corpse dust and torn apart. The boys took the gamble, sprinting alongside Wei Wuxian in pursuit of the sound. Sure enough, as they picked up the pace, the tapping shifted ahead of them, offering fleeting glimpses of a slight, petite shadow flitting through the white veil.

Jingyi jogged alongside him, calling out, "So we're just running away and leaving him?"

Wei Wuxian yelled back over his shoulder, "Hanguang-jun, he's all yours! We're heading ahead!"

A deep, twanging chord vibrated from the zither in the distance, sounding remarkably like a dry, spoken "Mm," which sent Wei Wuxian into a fit of muffled chuckles.

Jingyi scowled. "That's it? You're not going to say anything else?"

Wei Wuxian glanced over. "What else am I supposed to say?"

"You know—the usual! 'I'm worried about you, I have to stay!' 'No, you go!' 'Never, we leave together or not at all!' That sort of thing!"

Wei Wuxian nearly choked. "Where do you pick this melodrama up?! Who told you people talk like that? Setting me aside, can you actually picture your Hanguang-jun delivering a line like that with a straight face?"

The Lan disciples mumbled in unison, "No, definitely not..."

"Exactly," Wei Wuxian said. "Total waste of breath. Your Hanguang-jun is rock-solid; I know he can handle himself. My job is to keep you brats alive until we link back up."

Following the tapping through a labyrinth of sharp turns for barely half an incense stick, the sound abruptly vanished. Wei Wuxian held out an arm, halting the juniors. Creeping forward a few strides, a solitary building loomed through the thickening fog.

The front door groaned open on its hinges, waiting in silence for them to cross the threshold. Wei Wuxian had a hunch: something was waiting inside. Not a lethal trap, but the missing pieces to this entire puzzle.

"We're here anyway," he murmured. "Inside, everyone."

Stepping over the frame into the pitch-black interior, he warned without looking back, "Watch the threshold—don't trip."

One of the boys stumbled over the raised wood anyway, muttering, "Why on earth is this threshold built so high? It’s not like this is a temple."

"Not a temple," Wei Wuxian replied, "but definitely a place that needs one."

Sparks flared as five or six fire talismans flickered to life, bathing the hall in warm, dancing amber light.

Loose straw littered the floorboards. An altar table stood at the far end flanked by a cluster of mismatched wooden stools, with a pitch-black side chamber tucked to the right. Dominating the rest of the floor were seven or eight heavy, soot-black coffins.

Jin Ling’s brow furrowed. "Is this a mortuary? A place for dead bodies?"

"Yep," Wei Wuxian nodded. "Unclaimed corpses, unlucky deaths you can't keep at home, or bodies waiting for a burial plot all end up here. Think of it as a roadside inn for the dead." That dark side room was likely the caretaker's living quarters.

Lan Sizhui asked curiously, "Senior Mo, why do mortuaries build such high thresholds?"

"To keep the newly turned inside."

Lan Jingyi blinked. "A tall board of wood stops corpses from turning?"

"It doesn't stop them from turning," Wei Wuxian corrected, "but it keeps the low-grade ones from hopping out."

He turned around, standing right by the threshold. "Say I just died and turned into a fresh corpse."

The boys nodded eagerly.

"Freshly turned, my joints would be locked stiff, right? Zero flexibility?"

Jin Ling scoffed, "Obviously. You wouldn't even be able to bend your knees—you'd only be able to hop..." Mid-sentence, the lightbulb went off.

"Spot on," Wei Wuxian said. "You can only hop." He locked his ankles together and tried hopping forward; predictably, the towering wooden sill clipped his shins every single time, keeping him trapped inside.

Watching this grown man hop around like a ridiculous stiff had the boys cracking smiles, visualizing a freshly turned corpse fruitlessly bumping its toes against the timber.

"See that?" Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Don't laugh—it's folk wisdom. Primitive and a bit crude, sure, but remarkably effective against bottom-tier corpses. If it trips over the wood and hits the dirt, its locked joints keep it from getting back up quickly. By the time it manages to scramble upright, either the rooster's crowing at dawn or the caretaker's caught it. Ordinary folk coming up with practical survival tricks like that is pretty impressive."

Jin Ling, having caught himself smiling, snapped his scowl right back on. "Why did she bring us to a mortuary anyway? Is this place immune to walking corpses? And where did she vanish to?"

"It probably is immune," Wei Wuxian replied. "We've been standing here this whole time—have any of you heard a single corpse shuffling nearby?"

Right on cue, the ghostly form of the young maiden materialized atop one of the coffins.

Having already studied her terrifying visage under Wei Wuxian’s guidance—complete with bleeding sockets and a torn-out tongue—none of the boys flinched this time. Familiarity truly did breed courage.

Her spirit was intangible, bathed in a faint, ethereal glow. She had delicate features; cleaned up, she’d look like the sweet girl-next-door. But her posture was completely devoid of demure grace: legs splayed wide over the coffin, her makeshift bamboo cane leaning against the wood while her slender shins swung back and forth in frantic agitation.

She tapped the coffin lid urgently with her palm, then dropped to the floor, circling the casket while throwing rapid hand gestures at them. This time, the pantomime was unmistakable: she was mimicking the motion of sliding something open.

"She wants us to open this coffin?" Jin Ling asked.

Lan Sizhui murmured, "Could her remains be inside? Perhaps she wants us to give her a proper burial." It was the standard playbook for lingering spirits.

Wei Wuxian took up a position on one side of the casket. When a few boys moved to help, he waved them back. "Stay clear. On the off chance it's not a body and vents another blast of corpse dust, you'll catch it full in the face."

Heaving alone, he shoved the heavy wooden lid off, letting it thud against the straw. Peering inside, he found a body.

Except it wasn't the girl.

Lying inside was a young man laid out in peaceful repose, his hands clasped neatly over his chest over a horsehair whisk. Draped in spotless white Daoist robes, his lower jaw was sculpted with refined, scholarly grace, his skin pale and lips drained of color. But his upper face was bound in thick layers of linen; where his eyes should have rounded beneath the gauze, the fabric sank into hollow, flat depressions. There were no eyes beneath that wrap—only two empty sockets.

Hearing the casket open, the ghost girl stumbled over, her hands blindly combing through the air until her fingertips brushed the dead man's face. She stomped her feet, fresh tracks of blood weeping from her empty sockets.

No words or gestures were needed. Everyone understood instantly.

This corpse, discarded in the shadows of a lonely mortuary, was the real Xiao Xingchen.

A spirit's tears cannot fall to the earth. After weeping silently, she gritted her teeth and whipped around, making frantic, frustrated noises at the boys, practically bursting at the seams to tell them her story.

Lan Sizhui asked, "Should we useInquiryagain?"

"No," Wei Wuxian said. "We might not know the right questions to ask, and her story is going to be far too tangled for simple zither notes to untangle."

Though he hadn't saidyou can't handle it, Sizhui felt a small pang of inadequacy, quietly resolving to practiceInquiryuntil he could play it as flawlessly as Hanguang-jun.

Lan Jingyi frowned. "Then what do we do?"

"Empathy," Wei Wuxian answered.

Every major clan had their own methods for wringing intel from resentful spirits, but Empathy was Wei Wuxian’s signature craft. It wasn't gated by complex secret techniques: you simply invited the spirit to possess your vessel, turning your own body into a conduit to dive headfirst into the deceased's memories—seeing what they saw, hearing what they heard, feeling what they felt. If the spirit's emotional core was volatile enough, you’d be swept up in their raw grief, wrath, or mania; hence the name.

It was easily the most direct, rapid, and comprehensive technique available. And, naturally, the most perilous. Most cultivators avoided spirit possessions like the plague; Empathy was playing with fire, where a momentary lapse meant getting your soul hijacked or wiped out entirely.

Jin Ling protested, "That's way too dangerous! These crooked arts never—"

"We're out of time," Wei Wuxian cut him off. "Fall into formation. We wrap this up and get back to Hanguang-jun. Jin Ling, you're on watch."

A watcher was vital during Empathy to yank the medium out if they drowned in the spirit's memories. The tether required a pre-agreed signal—ideally a specific phrase or a sound intimately familiar to the medium.

Jin Ling pointed at his own chest. "Me? You wantmeto babysit you through this?"

Sizhui stepped forward. "If Young Master Jin would rather not, I can take it."

Wei Wuxian turned to Jin Ling. "Did you bring your Jiang clan clarity bell?"

The silver bell was a staple of the Yunmeng Jiang Sect. Raised between both clans, Jin Ling carried heirlooms from both Lotus Pier and Carp Tower. Wearing a conflicted expression, he pulled out a delicate antique bell engraved with the Jiang clan’s nine-petaled lotus.

Wei Wuxian handed it toward Sizhui. "The Jiang clan’s clarity bell clears the mind and grounds the spirit. Use it as the anchor."

Jin Ling snatched the bell right back. "I'll do it!"

Jingyi rolled his eyes. "First no, then yes—moody as a young mistress."

Wei Wuxian faced the girl. "Come on in."

Wiping her tear-streaked face, the ghost surged forward, diving headfirst into his chest. Wei Wuxian slid slowly down the side of the casket, his body going slack. The disciples scrambled to pile up armfuls of straw to cushion his fall, while Jin Ling gripped the silver bell white-knuckled, lost in thought.

As the spirit settled in, a sudden thought struck Wei Wuxian:Wait, the girl is blind. If I channel her memories, won't I be completely blind too? That ruins half the utility. Whatever, audio is better than nothing.

After a dizzying lurch of vertigo, his drifting consciousness snapped onto solid ground. The girl opened her eyes—and Wei Wuxian opened his along with her.

Instead of endless pitch-black, he was greeted by a sunlit landscape of rolling emerald hills and sparkling creeks.

He could actually see!

She wasn't blind yet at this point in her memories.

During Empathy, the medium experienced the strongest, most desperate memories the spirit wished to impart. Their senses were entirely shared: her eyes were his eyes, her lips his lips.

The girl was perched by a bubbling brook, using the water as a looking glass. Her clothes were ragged, but she clearly cared about keeping tidy. Tapping her foot to an idle tune, she pinned her hair up, fussing with it until she was satisfied—Wei Wuxian felt the slender wooden hairpin poking through her locks. Glancing down at the current, the reflection caught an oval face with a sharp, delicate chin.

Her eyes were completely devoid of pupils—solid, milky white.

Wei Wuxian frowned internally.She looks completely blind, yet I can see just fine?

Pleased with her hair, the girl hopped to her feet, scooped up her bamboo cane, and skipped down the country lane. She swung the stick wildly, smacking overhead leaves, kicking loose pebbles, and scattering grasshoppers from the weeds without a care in the world.

Spotting travelers approaching in the distance, she instantly dropped the bounce. Gripping the cane with delicate, practiced caution, she tapped the ground rhythmically, shuffling forward with fragile, hesitant steps. Several village maidens passed by, parting to give her a wide berth while murmuring sympathetically.

The girl nodded repeatedly. "Thank you, kind sisters, thank you!"

One of the village girls took pity on her, pulling a warm steamed bun from beneath the cloth of her basket and offering it over. "Careful on the road, little sister. Are you hungry? Take this."

The girl gasped softly, sounding overwhelmed. "Oh, I couldn't possibly... I, I..."

"Take it, go on!"

She took it with a bright, humble bow. "A-Qing thanks you, big sister!"

So her name was A-Qing.

Once the travelers were out of earshot, A-Qing scarfed the bun down in three bites and went right back to bouncing down the road. Trapped in her passenger seat, Wei Wuxian was getting motion sickness from all the leaping.This girl is wild. Ah, I get it now: she faked it. Born with milky eyes, she looked blind at a glance, so she weaponized it to con handouts and duck suspicion.A lone girl roaming the world needed an edge; acting helpless let people drop their guard while she watched everything like a hawk. Pretty clever survival strategy.

Yet her ghost had been genuinely sightless, meaning she had lost her eyes before she died. How did she go from faking it to the real thing?

Did she see something she wasn't supposed to?

She hopped when alone and played the fragile blind beggar whenever crowds appeared, eventually wandering into a bustling town market.

With so many marks around, she put on a masterclass, tapping her stick with exaggerated frailty. Shuffling through the throng, she suddenly threw herself right into the chest of a well-dressed middle-aged man, crying out in sheer terror, "I'm so sorry, I'm so sorry! I couldn't see, forgive me!"

Couldn't see, my foot—she’d lined him up from ten paces away!

The man whirled around, ready to curse her out. But spotting a pretty, sightless waif, he bit his tongue to avoid making a public scene, settling for a harsh growl: "Watch where you're going!"

A-Qing bowed frantically in apology. Before turning away, the man casually reached out and gave her backside a crude, heavy pinch. Experiencing the grope firsthand, Wei Wuxian’s skin crawled with a massive wave of disgust, itching to bury the creep ten feet under the flagstones.

A-Qing shrank back, feigning terrified meekness. But the second the man vanished around the corner, she slipped into an alleyway, spat on the dirt, and fished a silk coin pouch from her bodice. Counting the coppers, she spat again in disgust. "Filthy scumbag. Dressed to the nines and barely carrying two coins to rub together. Squeeze him dry and he wouldn't even rattle."

Wei Wuxian didn't know whether to laugh or cry. She wasn't even fifteen, yet her tongue was razor-sharp and her pickpocketing was second nature.If you'd tried lifting from me back in the day, you wouldn't be complaining—I used to be rolling in coin.

While he was reminiscing about how he’d ended up a broke vagrant, A-Qing had already picked her next mark. Shuffling back into the street with her cane, she ran the exact same routine, throwing herself with an "Aiyoh!" right into the arms of a white-robed Daoist. "I'm sorry, I'm so sorry! I couldn't see, forgive me!"

Wei Wuxian groaned internally.You didn't even bother changing the script, kid!

The impact bumped the Daoist back half a step. Steadying her gently by the elbows, a warm, calm voice asked, "I take no harm. Are you unable to see as well, young lady?"

He was young, dressed in modest, immaculate white robes, with a longsword wrapped in white linen strapped across his back. His lower face was handsome and delicate, if a little lean.

His upper face was bound in thick white gauze—stained faintly with the seep of old blood.
